notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Motion is the change in position of an object with time relative to a reference point.
  • Rest and motion are relative concepts.
  • An object may be at rest with respect to one observer and in motion with respect to another.
  • Motion is described using position, distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration.
  • The SI unit of length is metre.
  • The SI unit of time is second.
  • Motion may be uniform or non-uniform.
  • Motion may be translational, rotational, circular, oscillatory, periodic or random.
  • Kinematics is the branch of mechanics that describes motion without studying its causes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Motion → Change in Position with Time

2. Reference Point
  • A reference point is a fixed point relative to which position or motion is described.
  • Motion cannot be meaningfully described without a frame or reference point.
  • A passenger sitting inside a moving train is at rest relative to the train.
  • The same passenger is moving relative to a person standing on the ground.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Rest and motion are relative, not absolute in ordinary mechanics.

3. Position
  • Position describes the location of an object relative to a chosen origin.
  • Position may be described using coordinates.
  • Change in position gives displacement.
  • Position can be positive, negative or zero depending on the chosen coordinate system.
4. Distance
  • Distance is the total length of the actual path travelled by an object.
  • Distance is a scalar quantity.
  • Distance has magnitude only.
  • Distance is always zero or positive.
  • SI unit of distance is metre.
  • Distance travelled depends on the actual path followed.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Distance → Actual Path → Scalar

5. Displacement
  • Displacement is the shortest straight-line change from initial position to final position.
  • Displacement is a vector quantity.
  • Displacement has both magnitude and direction.
  • SI unit is metre.
  • Displacement can be positive, negative or zero in one-dimensional motion.
  • Displacement depends only on initial and final positions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Displacement → Shortest Directed Change → Vector

6. Distance vs Displacement
  • Distance is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement.
  • Distance can never be negative.
  • Displacement can be zero even when distance is non-zero.
  • For straight-line motion without change of direction, distance equals magnitude of displacement.
  • For a complete round trip, displacement is zero but distance is not zero.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Round trip → Displacement = 0

Distance ≠ 0

7. Example — Circular Track
  • A runner completing one full lap returns to the starting point.
  • Displacement after one complete lap is zero.
  • Distance equals the circumference of the track.
  • After half a circular lap, displacement equals the diameter of the circle.
8. Speed
  • Speed is the rate of change of distance.
  • Speed = Distance / Time.
  • Speed is a scalar quantity.
  • SI unit of speed is metre per second.
  • Speed cannot be negative in elementary mechanics.
  • An object at rest has zero speed.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Speed → Distance/Time → Scalar

9. Velocity
  • Velocity is the rate of change of displacement.
  • Velocity = Displacement / Time for average velocity.
  • Instantaneous velocity gives rate of change of position at a particular instant.
  • Velocity is a vector quantity.
  • SI unit is metre per second.
  • Velocity changes if either speed or direction changes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Velocity → Displacement/Time → Vector

10. Speed vs Velocity
  • Speed is scalar.
  • Velocity is vector.
  • Speed uses distance.
  • Velocity uses displacement.
  • Constant speed does not necessarily mean constant velocity.
  • In uniform circular motion, speed is constant but velocity changes continuously.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Constant speed in a circle → Velocity not constant.

11. Average Speed
  • Average speed = Total distance travelled / Total time taken.
  • Average speed depends on total path length.
  • Average speed is not generally equal to the arithmetic mean of two speeds.
  • Equal distances travelled at different speeds require special treatment.
12. Average Speed for Equal Distances
  • If equal distances are travelled at speeds u and v, average speed = 2uv/(u + v).
  • The arithmetic mean is valid only in special cases such as equal time intervals.
📌 Remember

Equal distance average speed → Harmonic-type mean

2uv/(u + v)

13. Average Velocity
  • Average velocity = Total displacement / Total time.
  • Average velocity can be zero even when the object has travelled a considerable distance.
  • For a closed journey returning to the start, average velocity is zero.
  • Average speed is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of average velocity.
14. Instantaneous Speed
  • Instantaneous speed is the speed at a particular instant.
  • A vehicle speedometer shows instantaneous speed.
  • Instantaneous speed is the magnitude of instantaneous velocity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Speedometer → Instantaneous Speed

15. Uniform Motion
  • Uniform motion means an object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.
  • In uniform straight-line motion, velocity remains constant.
  • Acceleration is zero in uniform rectilinear motion.
  • A distance-time graph for uniform motion is a straight line with constant slope.
📌 Remember

Uniform Straight-Line Motion → Constant Velocity → a = 0

16. Non-Uniform Motion
  • Non-uniform motion occurs when unequal distances are covered in equal time intervals or direction changes.
  • Speed or velocity changes with time.
  • Accelerated motion is a form of non-uniform motion.
  • Circular motion at constant speed is non-uniform velocity motion because direction changes.
17. Acceleration
  • Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
  • a = (v − u)/t for constant acceleration.
  • Acceleration is a vector quantity.
  • SI unit is m/s².
  • Acceleration can result from change in speed, direction or both.
  • Positive acceleration increases velocity in the chosen positive direction.
  • Negative acceleration may correspond to slowing down depending on the direction of motion.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Acceleration → Change in Velocity / Time

18. Retardation / Deceleration
  • Retardation or deceleration commonly refers to acceleration opposite to the direction of motion.
  • Deceleration reduces speed.
  • It is often represented as negative acceleration in a coordinate system where motion is positive.
  • Braking of a vehicle produces deceleration.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down.

It depends on the chosen direction and sign of velocity.

19. Uniform Acceleration
  • Uniform acceleration means velocity changes by equal amounts in equal time intervals.
  • Acceleration remains constant.
  • Freely falling objects near Earth's surface approximately have uniform acceleration when air resistance is neglected.
  • Standard equations of motion apply to constant acceleration.
20. Non-Uniform Acceleration
  • Non-uniform acceleration changes with time.
  • A car moving through city traffic generally has non-uniform acceleration.
  • Acceleration may change in magnitude or direction.
  • Circular motion has continuously changing acceleration direction if the path changes.
21. Equations of Motion

For constant acceleration in a straight line:

  • v = u + at.
  • s = ut + ½at².
  • v² = u² + 2as.
  • s = (u + v)t/2.

Where:

  • u = Initial velocity.
  • v = Final velocity.
  • a = Acceleration.
  • t = Time.
  • s = Displacement.
📌 Must-Memorise

v = u + at

s = ut + ½at²

v² = u² + 2as

22. First Equation of Motion
  • v = u + at.
  • It relates initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration and time.
  • It applies to constant acceleration.
  • If a = 0, then v = u.
23. Second Equation of Motion
  • s = ut + ½at².
  • It gives displacement under constant acceleration.
  • For a body starting from rest, u = 0 and s = ½at².
24. Third Equation of Motion
  • v² = u² + 2as.
  • This equation does not explicitly contain time.
  • It is useful when displacement and velocity are known.
25. Distance-Time Graph
  • Distance is plotted on the vertical axis.
  • Time is plotted on the horizontal axis.
  • Slope of a distance-time graph gives speed.
  • A horizontal line indicates zero speed.
  • A steeper slope indicates greater speed.
  • A straight inclined line indicates constant speed.
  • A curved line indicates changing speed.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Distance-Time Graph Slope → Speed

26. Displacement-Time Graph
  • Slope of a displacement-time graph gives velocity.
  • Positive slope indicates positive velocity.
  • Negative slope indicates negative velocity.
  • Zero slope indicates rest.
  • Constant slope indicates constant velocity.
  • Changing slope indicates acceleration.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Displacement-Time Slope → Velocity

27. Velocity-Time Graph
  • Velocity is plotted against time.
  • Slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration.
  • Area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.
  • Horizontal line indicates constant velocity.
  • Upward straight slope indicates constant positive acceleration.
  • Downward straight slope indicates constant negative acceleration.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

v–t Slope → Acceleration

v–t Area → Displacement

28. Speed-Time Graph
  • Slope of a speed-time graph gives rate of change of speed.
  • Area under a speed-time graph gives distance travelled.
  • Unlike velocity-time graphs, speed is not signed negative in elementary treatment.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Area under speed-time → Distance.

Area under velocity-time → Displacement.

29. Acceleration-Time Graph
  • Area under an acceleration-time graph gives change in velocity.
  • A horizontal line above zero indicates constant positive acceleration.
  • A line on the time axis indicates zero acceleration.
  • Negative acceleration lies below the time axis in the chosen sign convention.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

a–t Area → Change in Velocity

30. Graph Summary
  • Distance-time slope → Speed.
  • Displacement-time slope → Velocity.
  • Velocity-time slope → Acceleration.
  • Velocity-time area → Displacement.
  • Speed-time area → Distance.
  • Acceleration-time area → Change in velocity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Graph Questions → Slope or Area

31. Scalar Quantities in Motion
  • Distance is scalar.
  • Speed is scalar.
  • Time is scalar.
  • Path length is scalar.
32. Vector Quantities in Motion
  • Displacement is vector.
  • Velocity is vector.
  • Acceleration is vector.
  • Position vector is vector.
33. Translational Motion
  • Translational motion occurs when a body moves from one position to another.
  • Every point of a body undergoes the same displacement in pure translation.
  • Translational motion may be rectilinear or curvilinear.
34. Rectilinear Motion
  • Rectilinear motion occurs along a straight line.
  • A lift moving vertically is approximately rectilinear.
  • A train moving on a straight track shows rectilinear motion.
  • One-dimensional equations of motion are especially useful here.
35. Curvilinear Motion
  • Curvilinear motion occurs along a curved path.
  • Projectile motion is curvilinear.
  • Motion of a vehicle around a bend is curvilinear.
  • Circular motion is a special case of curvilinear motion.
36. Rotational Motion
  • Rotational motion is motion about an axis.
  • Every point of a rigid rotating body moves in a circle around the axis.
  • A rotating fan exhibits rotational motion.
  • Earth's rotation about its axis is rotational motion.
37. Circular Motion
  • Circular motion occurs along a circular path.
  • Uniform circular motion has constant speed.
  • Velocity changes continuously because its direction changes.
  • Circular motion therefore involves acceleration.
  • Centripetal acceleration acts toward the centre.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Uniform circular motion → Speed constant, velocity changing.

38. Centripetal Acceleration
  • Centripetal acceleration is directed toward the centre of a circular path.
  • a = v²/r.
  • It can also be written as a = rω².
  • Larger speed produces larger centripetal acceleration.
  • Larger radius reduces centripetal acceleration for the same linear speed.
39. Centripetal Force
  • Centripetal force is the inward resultant force producing circular motion.
  • F = mv²/r.
  • It is not a separate fundamental force.
  • Tension may provide centripetal force.
  • Friction may provide centripetal force.
  • Gravity may provide centripetal force.
40. Tangential Velocity
  • Tangential velocity is directed along the tangent to a circular path.
  • If centripetal force suddenly disappears, the object moves approximately along the tangent.
  • Tangential speed is related to angular speed by v = rω.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Circular motion release → Tangential direction

41. Angular Displacement
  • Angular displacement is the angle through which a body rotates.
  • SI unit is radian.
  • One complete revolution corresponds to 2π radians.
  • 360° = 2π rad.
  • 180° = π rad.
42. Angular Velocity
  • Angular velocity is rate of change of angular displacement.
  • ω = θ/t for uniform angular motion.
  • SI unit is rad/s.
  • Linear speed and angular velocity are related by v = rω.
43. Angular Acceleration
  • Angular acceleration is rate of change of angular velocity.
  • It is commonly represented by α.
  • SI unit is rad/s².
  • Constant angular acceleration is the rotational analogue of constant linear acceleration.
44. Periodic Motion
  • Periodic motion repeats itself after equal intervals of time.
  • Earth's revolution around the Sun is approximately periodic.
  • Oscillation of a simple pendulum is periodic for small amplitudes.
  • Rotation of a wheel at constant angular speed is periodic.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Periodic Motion → Repeats at Regular Intervals

45. Oscillatory Motion
  • Oscillatory motion is repeated to-and-fro motion about an equilibrium position.
  • A simple pendulum oscillates.
  • A mass attached to a spring can oscillate.
  • Oscillatory motion is often periodic.
  • Not every periodic motion is oscillatory.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

All oscillatory periodic motions are periodic under ideal conditions, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory.

46. Simple Harmonic Motion
  • Simple harmonic motion is oscillatory motion with restoring acceleration proportional to displacement and directed toward equilibrium.
  • a ∝ −x.
  • A mass-spring system can execute SHM.
  • A simple pendulum approximates SHM for small angular displacement.
  • Velocity is maximum at equilibrium position.
  • Acceleration is zero at equilibrium.
  • Velocity is zero at extreme positions.
  • Acceleration magnitude is maximum at extremes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

SHM Centre → v max, a = 0

SHM Extremes → v = 0, a max

47. Time Period
  • Time period is time taken for one complete cycle.
  • It is represented by T.
  • SI unit is second.
  • T = 1/f.
48. Frequency
  • Frequency is the number of complete cycles per second.
  • It is represented by f.
  • SI unit is hertz.
  • 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second.
  • f = 1/T.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Frequency × Time Period = 1

49. Simple Pendulum
  • A simple pendulum consists ideally of a point mass suspended by a light string.
  • For small oscillations, T = 2π√(L/g).
  • Period depends on length.
  • Period depends on gravitational acceleration.
  • Period does not depend on mass of the bob in the ideal model.
  • Longer pendulum has longer time period.
50. Random Motion
  • Random motion has no fixed predictable path at the microscopic level.
  • Brownian motion is a classic example.
  • Gas molecules move randomly.
  • Random motion differs from regular periodic motion.
51. Brownian Motion
  • Brownian motion is the random movement of small particles suspended in a fluid.
  • It is caused by collisions with molecules of the fluid.
  • Robert Brown observed the phenomenon in 1827.
  • Brownian motion supports the molecular theory of matter.
52. Projectile Motion
  • Projectile motion is the motion of an object after launch under gravity alone, neglecting air resistance.
  • Horizontal and vertical motions are independent in the ideal model.
  • Horizontal velocity remains constant.
  • Vertical velocity changes due to gravity.
  • The trajectory is parabolic.
  • Acceleration is always g downward.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Projectile → Horizontal constant + Vertical accelerated

53. Projectile at Highest Point
  • Vertical velocity becomes zero at the highest point.
  • Horizontal velocity remains unchanged in the ideal model.
  • Acceleration remains g downward.
  • Total velocity is not zero unless horizontal velocity is also zero.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Highest point → v_y = 0

But acceleration ≠ 0

54. Time of Flight

For projectile launched and landing at the same level:

  • Time of flight T = 2u sinθ/g.
  • It increases with vertical component of launch velocity.
  • Maximum time of flight for fixed u occurs at 90°.
55. Maximum Height of Projectile
  • Maximum height H = u² sin²θ / 2g.
  • Greater vertical launch component produces greater height.
  • Maximum height for a fixed launch speed occurs at 90°.
56. Horizontal Range
  • For launch and landing at same level, range R = u² sin2θ/g.
  • Maximum range occurs at 45°.
  • Complementary angles θ and 90° − θ give the same range for the same launch speed.
  • Range is zero for 0° and 90° under same-level ideal conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Maximum Projectile Range → 45°

57. Horizontal Projectile
  • A horizontally projected body has initial vertical velocity zero.
  • Horizontal velocity remains constant in the ideal model.
  • Vertical displacement follows free-fall motion.
  • The trajectory is parabolic.
58. Free Fall
  • Free fall is motion under gravity alone.
  • Near Earth's surface, acceleration due to gravity is approximately 9.8 m/s².
  • In vacuum, all objects fall with the same g at the same location.
  • Falling speed differences in air arise mainly from air resistance.
  • Galileo's experiments contributed to understanding free fall.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mass does not affect free-fall acceleration in vacuum.

59. Equations for Free Fall

Taking downward as positive:

  • v = u + gt.
  • s = ut + ½gt².
  • v² = u² + 2gs.
  • For a body dropped from rest, u = 0.
60. Body Thrown Vertically Upward
  • Initial velocity is upward.
  • Gravitational acceleration acts downward.
  • Speed decreases as the body rises.
  • Velocity becomes zero momentarily at maximum height.
  • Acceleration remains g downward at the top.
  • The body then accelerates downward.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

At highest point:

Velocity = 0

Acceleration = g downward

61. Time to Reach Maximum Height
  • For vertical upward projection, t = u/g.
  • Maximum height H = u²/2g.
  • Ignoring air resistance, total time to return to same level = 2u/g.
62. Relative Motion
  • Relative motion describes motion of one object as observed from another moving object.
  • Relative velocity is the difference between velocities in one-dimensional motion.
  • If two objects move in the same direction, relative speed is the difference of speeds.
  • If they move in opposite directions, relative speed is the sum of speeds.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Same Direction → Difference

Opposite Direction → Sum

63. Relative Velocity
  • Velocity of A relative to B is vAB = vA − vB.
  • Relative velocity is a vector.
  • If both have the same velocity, relative velocity is zero.
  • A passenger in two trains moving side by side at equal velocity may appear stationary relative to the other train.
64. Relative Speed — Trains
  • Two trains moving toward each other have relative speed equal to the sum of their speeds.
  • Two trains moving in the same direction have relative speed equal to the difference of speeds.
  • This principle is frequently used in train-crossing problems.
65. Unit Conversion — km/h and m/s
  • To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18.
  • To convert m/s to km/h, multiply by 18/5.
  • 36 km/h = 10 m/s.
  • 72 km/h = 20 m/s.
  • 54 km/h = 15 m/s.
  • 90 km/h = 25 m/s.
📌 Must-Memorise

km/h → m/s = × 5/18

m/s → km/h = × 18/5

66. Uniform Velocity
  • Uniform velocity means both magnitude and direction remain constant.
  • The object covers equal displacements in equal time intervals in the same direction.
  • Uniform velocity requires straight-line motion.
  • Acceleration is zero.
67. Variable Velocity
  • Velocity is variable if speed changes.
  • Velocity is also variable if direction changes.
  • Circular motion has variable velocity even at constant speed.
  • Any acceleration implies changing velocity.
68. Average Speed Cannot Exceed Maximum Speed
  • Average speed must lie between the minimum and maximum speeds experienced over the journey.
  • It cannot exceed the maximum instantaneous speed.
  • It need not equal the arithmetic mean of maximum and minimum speeds.
69. Uniform Circular Motion
  • Speed remains constant.
  • Velocity direction changes continuously.
  • Acceleration is directed toward the centre.
  • Net inward force is required.
  • Work done by ideal centripetal force is zero because it is perpendicular to instantaneous displacement.
70. Revolution vs Rotation
  • Rotation is spinning about an internal axis.
  • Revolution is orbital motion around another object.
  • Earth rotates on its axis.
  • Earth revolves around the Sun.
  • Earth's rotation causes day and night.
  • Earth's revolution together with axial tilt causes seasons.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rotation → Day/Night

Revolution + Tilt → Seasons

71. Earth's Rotation
  • Earth rotates from west to east.
  • One solar day is approximately 24 hours.
  • Earth's eastward rotation makes the Sun appear to move east-to-west across the sky.
  • Rotation causes the daily cycle of day and night.
72. Earth's Revolution
  • Earth revolves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit.
  • One revolution takes approximately 365¼ days.
  • A leap year compensates approximately for the extra quarter day.
  • Earth's orbital motion follows Kepler's laws.
73. Uniform Motion Graph Trap
  • A straight horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the object is at rest.
  • A straight inclined distance-time graph means constant speed.
  • A horizontal velocity-time graph above zero means constant velocity.
  • A horizontal acceleration-time graph at zero means no acceleration.
74. Negative Velocity
  • Negative velocity indicates motion in the direction chosen as negative.
  • It does not mean the object is necessarily slowing down.
  • Negative sign shows direction.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Negative velocity ≠ negative speed.

Speed is non-negative.

75. Negative Acceleration
  • Negative acceleration means acceleration in the chosen negative direction.
  • If velocity is positive, negative acceleration can reduce speed.
  • If velocity is negative, negative acceleration can increase speed magnitude.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Negative acceleration ≠ always deceleration.

76. Motion and Inertia
  • An object in uniform straight-line motion continues that motion if net external force is zero.
  • This follows Newton's First Law.
  • Force is required to change velocity, not to maintain constant velocity in an ideal frictionless system.
77. Motion and Momentum
  • Momentum = Mass × Velocity.
  • Momentum changes when velocity changes.
  • Force equals rate of change of momentum.
  • Momentum is conserved in an isolated system.
78. Motion and Force
  • Net force produces acceleration.
  • Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
  • For constant mass, F = ma.
  • Greater force gives greater acceleration for the same mass.
  • Greater mass gives smaller acceleration for the same force.
79. Motion and Energy
  • A moving body possesses kinetic energy.
  • KE = ½mv².
  • Kinetic energy depends on the square of speed.
  • Doubling speed makes kinetic energy four times greater for the same mass.
  • Motion can be changed when work is done on a body.
80. Motion in Vacuum
  • In vacuum there is no air resistance.
  • All freely falling bodies at the same location accelerate equally.
  • A feather and hammer fall together in vacuum.
  • Air resistance explains different falling rates in ordinary air.
81. Galileo and Motion
  • Galileo Galilei made major contributions to the scientific study of motion.
  • He studied falling bodies.
  • He studied accelerated motion.
  • He studied projectile motion.
  • His work laid foundations for kinematics.
  • Galileo challenged the belief that heavier objects necessarily fall faster.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Galileo → Falling Bodies + Acceleration + Projectile Motion

82. Newton and Motion
  • Isaac Newton formulated three laws of motion.
  • Newton's First Law deals with inertia.
  • Newton's Second Law relates force and acceleration.
  • Newton's Third Law deals with action and reaction.
  • Newton's laws form the foundation of classical mechanics.
83. Speedometer
  • A speedometer measures instantaneous speed of a vehicle.
  • It does not directly measure distance travelled.
  • The SI unit of speed is m/s, although vehicle speedometers commonly display km/h.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Speedometer → Speed

84. Odometer
  • An odometer records distance travelled by a vehicle.
  • It does not measure instantaneous speed.
  • Odometer and speedometer perform different functions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Speedometer → Speed

Odometer → Distance

85. Tachometer
  • A tachometer measures rotational speed.
  • It is commonly used to display engine revolutions per minute.
  • RPM means revolutions per minute.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tachometer → Rotational Speed / RPM

86. Accelerometer
  • An accelerometer measures acceleration.
  • Accelerometers are used in smartphones, vehicles and navigation systems.
  • They can detect changes in orientation and motion when used with other sensors.
87. Uniform Acceleration Graph
  • In a velocity-time graph, constant acceleration gives a straight line.
  • The slope equals acceleration.
  • Increasing positive slope indicates greater positive acceleration.
  • Zero slope means zero acceleration.
88. Rest
  • An object is at rest when its position does not change with time relative to the chosen reference frame.
  • Rest is relative.
  • A person sitting in a moving bus is at rest relative to the bus but moving relative to the road.
89. Motion Classification — Must Remember
  • Straight-line motion → Rectilinear.
  • Curved-path motion → Curvilinear.
  • Circular path → Circular motion.
  • About an axis → Rotational motion.
  • Repeated after fixed intervals → Periodic motion.
  • To-and-fro about mean position → Oscillatory motion.
  • Irregular unpredictable path → Random motion.
90. Important Motion Formulae
  • Speed = Distance/Time.
  • Average speed = Total distance/Total time.
  • Average velocity = Total displacement/Total time.
  • Acceleration = Change in velocity/Time.
  • v = u + at.
  • s = ut + ½at².
  • v² = u² + 2as.
  • s = (u + v)t/2.
  • Centripetal acceleration = v²/r.
  • Centripetal force = mv²/r.
  • Angular velocity = θ/t.
  • Linear speed = rω.
  • Frequency = 1/T.
  • Projectile time of flight = 2u sinθ/g.
  • Projectile maximum height = u²sin²θ/2g.
  • Projectile range = u²sin2θ/g.
91. Important SI Units
  • Distance → metre.
  • Displacement → metre.
  • Speed → m/s.
  • Velocity → m/s.
  • Acceleration → m/s².
  • Time → second.
  • Angular displacement → radian.
  • Angular velocity → rad/s.
  • Angular acceleration → rad/s².
  • Frequency → hertz.
  • Time period → second.
92. Must-Memorise Motion Pairs
  • Distance → Scalar.
  • Displacement → Vector.
  • Speed → Scalar.
  • Velocity → Vector.
  • Acceleration → Vector.
  • Speedometer → Speed.
  • Odometer → Distance.
  • Tachometer → RPM.
  • Accelerometer → Acceleration.
  • Distance-time slope → Speed.
  • Displacement-time slope → Velocity.
  • Velocity-time slope → Acceleration.
  • Velocity-time area → Displacement.
  • Speed-time area → Distance.
  • Acceleration-time area → Change in velocity.
93. TNPSC Traps
  • Motion requires a reference point.
  • Distance can be non-zero while displacement is zero.
  • Distance is scalar.
  • Displacement is vector.
  • Speed is scalar.
  • Velocity is vector.
  • Average speed is not always arithmetic mean of speeds.
  • Average velocity can be zero while average speed is non-zero.
  • Constant speed does not always mean constant velocity.
  • Uniform circular motion has acceleration.
  • Acceleration can occur due only to change in direction.
  • Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down.
  • A distance-time graph slope gives speed.
  • A displacement-time graph slope gives velocity.
  • Velocity-time slope gives acceleration.
  • Velocity-time area gives displacement.
  • Speed-time area gives distance.
  • At the highest point of a projectile, vertical velocity is zero but acceleration is g downward.
  • Maximum projectile range on level ground occurs at 45°.
  • Complementary projectile angles have equal range under ideal conditions.
  • In vacuum, mass does not affect free-fall acceleration.
  • At maximum height of vertical throw, acceleration is not zero.
  • Speedometer measures speed.
  • Odometer measures distance.
  • Tachometer measures rotational speed.
  • Relative speed in opposite directions is the sum.
  • Relative speed in same direction is the difference.
94. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Motion → Position changes.
  • Distance → Path.
  • Displacement → Shortest directed change.
  • Speed → Distance/time.
  • Velocity → Displacement/time.
  • Acceleration → Δv/t.
  • Uniform motion → Constant speed.
  • Uniform velocity → Straight line + constant speed.
  • v = u + at.
  • s = ut + ½at².
  • v² = u² + 2as.
  • d–t slope → Speed.
  • x–t slope → Velocity.
  • v–t slope → Acceleration.
  • v–t area → Displacement.
  • Circular motion → Centripetal acceleration.
  • SHM centre → v max.
  • SHM extreme → a max.
  • Projectile → Parabola.
  • Range max → 45°.
  • Free fall → g.
  • Same-direction relative speed → Difference.
  • Opposite-direction relative speed → Sum.
  • km/h to m/s → ×5/18.
  • m/s to km/h → ×18/5.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • Motion means? → Change in position with time relative to a reference point.
  • Is motion absolute? → No, it is relative to a reference frame.
  • Total actual path travelled? → Distance.
  • Shortest directed change between initial and final positions? → Displacement.
  • Distance is? → Scalar.
  • Displacement is? → Vector.
  • Can displacement be zero when distance is non-zero? → Yes.
  • One complete circular lap gives displacement? → Zero.
  • Rate of change of distance? → Speed.
  • Rate of change of displacement? → Velocity.
  • Speed is? → Scalar.
  • Velocity is? → Vector.
  • SI unit of speed and velocity? → m/s.
  • Average speed formula? → Total distance / Total time.
  • Average velocity formula? → Total displacement / Total time.
  • For a complete round trip, average velocity? → Zero.
  • Instantaneous speed measured by? → Speedometer.
  • Distance travelled by vehicle recorded by? → Odometer.
  • Rotational speed measured by? → Tachometer.
  • Acceleration measured by? → Accelerometer.
  • Rate of change of velocity? → Acceleration.
  • SI unit of acceleration? → m/s².
  • Can direction change cause acceleration? → Yes.
  • Uniform straight-line motion has acceleration? → Zero.
  • First equation of motion? → v = u + at.
  • Second equation? → s = ut + ½at².
  • Third equation? → v² = u² + 2as.
  • Equations of motion require? → Constant acceleration.
  • Slope of distance-time graph? → Speed.
  • Slope of displacement-time graph? → Velocity.
  • Slope of velocity-time graph? → Acceleration.
  • Area under velocity-time graph? → Displacement.
  • Area under speed-time graph? → Distance.
  • Area under acceleration-time graph? → Change in velocity.
  • Straight horizontal distance-time graph means? → Rest.
  • Straight inclined distance-time graph means? → Constant speed.
  • Motion along straight line? → Rectilinear motion.
  • Motion along curved path? → Curvilinear motion.
  • Motion about an axis? → Rotational motion.
  • Motion repeating after equal intervals? → Periodic motion.
  • To-and-fro motion about equilibrium? → Oscillatory motion.
  • Constant-speed circular motion has constant velocity? → No.
  • Direction of centripetal acceleration? → Toward the centre.
  • Centripetal acceleration formula? → v²/r.
  • Centripetal force formula? → mv²/r.
  • Linear-angular speed relation? → v = rω.
  • One revolution in radians? → 2π radians.
  • 180° equals? → π radians.
  • Frequency formula? → f = 1/T.
  • SI unit of frequency? → Hertz.
  • Time period SI unit? → Second.
  • At centre of SHM, velocity? → Maximum.
  • At centre of SHM, acceleration? → Zero.
  • At extreme of SHM, velocity? → Zero.
  • At extreme of SHM, acceleration magnitude? → Maximum.
  • Simple pendulum period? → 2π√(L/g).
  • Does pendulum period depend on bob mass? → No, ideally.
  • Projectile trajectory? → Parabola.
  • Projectile horizontal acceleration in ideal model? → Zero.
  • Projectile vertical acceleration? → g downward.
  • At highest point of projectile, vertical velocity? → Zero.
  • At highest point, acceleration? → g downward.
  • Projectile maximum range angle? → 45°.
  • Projectile range formula? → u² sin2θ/g.
  • Time of flight formula? → 2u sinθ/g.
  • Maximum height formula? → u²sin²θ/2g.
  • Free fall means? → Motion under gravity alone.
  • Acceleration due to gravity near Earth? → About 9.8 m/s².
  • Do heavy and light bodies fall with same g in vacuum? → Yes.
  • Body thrown vertically upward at highest point has velocity? → Zero.
  • Acceleration at highest point? → g downward.
  • Time to maximum height? → u/g.
  • Maximum height for vertical throw? → u²/2g.
  • Relative speed in same direction? → Difference of speeds.
  • Relative speed in opposite directions? → Sum of speeds.
  • Convert km/h to m/s? → Multiply by 5/18.
  • Convert m/s to km/h? → Multiply by 18/5.
  • 36 km/h equals? → 10 m/s.
  • 72 km/h equals? → 20 m/s.
  • 54 km/h equals? → 15 m/s.
  • 90 km/h equals? → 25 m/s.
  • Scientist strongly associated with experiments on falling bodies? → Galileo Galilei.
  • Scientist who formulated laws of motion? → Isaac Newton.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Distance → Scalar; Displacement → Vector; Speed → Scalar; Velocity → Vector; Acceleration → Δv/t; v–t slope → a; v–t area → displacement.
